JM-01.name: Cook
JM-01.caption: Trump v. Cook — SCOTUS No. 25A312; below D.D.C. and D.C. Circuit
JM-01.question: May the President immediately remove a sitting Fed Governor "for cause," without notice and a chance to answer — and is the Governor's tenure protection constitutional?
JM-01.state: Stay denied 2026-06-29. Fed Governor for-cause protection held constitutional; removal requires notice and an opportunity to respond. Cook keeps her seat and votes while the merits continue below.
JM-01.stakes: One Governor's chair is one FOMC vote — and the ruling drew the constitutional fence around the Fed itself: the one agency the removal revolution doesn't reach.

JM-02.name: Slaughter
JM-02.caption: Trump v. Slaughter — SCOTUS No. 25-332; below D.D.C.
JM-02.question: Does the FTC's for-cause removal protection survive Article II?
JM-02.state: Reversed 6–3 on 2026-06-29: FTC protection unconstitutional; Humphrey's Executor no longer shields the modern commission. The Fed was expressly treated as a distinct historical arrangement.
JM-02.stakes: Every independent financial commission except the Fed is now removable at will — the President's hand reaches SEC-style bodies, and only the central bank keeps its carve-out.

JM-03.name: CFPB funding
JM-03.caption: CFPB v. Community Financial Services Ass'n — SCOTUS No. 22-448 (2024)
JM-03.question: Is the CFPB's capped draw from the Federal Reserve a valid appropriation?
JM-03.state: Upheld 7–2 (2024): a standing source-and-purpose appropriation satisfies the Appropriations Clause.
JM-03.stakes: Self-funding through the Fed is constitutional in principle — which made the later fight (JM-04) about starving the channel in practice, not its legality.

JM-04.name: NTEU v. Vought
JM-04.caption: NTEU v. Vought — D.D.C. 1:25-cv-00381; D.C. Cir. 25-5091 & 26-5220 (en banc)
JM-04.question: May the executive stop work, refuse funding, cancel contracts, and RIF an agency Congress created — and can courts stop it?
JM-04.state: Preliminary restraints partly hold; panel vacatur wiped by en banc grant; 2026-06-19 limited remand with jurisdiction retained. No final rule on how small the CFPB may lawfully become.
JM-04.stakes: The live test of whether an agency can be killed by management rather than statute — the purse fenced but not filled.

JM-05.name: Consumers' Research
JM-05.caption: FCC v. Consumers' Research — SCOTUS No. 24-354 (2025)
JM-05.question: Did Congress unconstitutionally delegate revenue power over the Universal Service Fund, or the FCC subdelegate it to a private administrator?
JM-05.state: Upheld 6–3 (2025): adequate guidance, agency retains final say, private role advisory only.
JM-05.stakes: The public-regulator/private-administrator funding machine survives — the closest analogue blessing hybrid money plumbing run through private bodies.

JM-06.name: Custodia
JM-06.caption: Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board & FRB Kansas City — D. Wyo.; 10th Cir. 24-8024; SCOTUS No. 26-62
JM-06.question: Does statutory eligibility give a state-chartered bank a right to a Reserve Bank master account?
JM-06.state: Tenth Circuit: no — Reserve Banks keep discretion to deny eligible institutions. Cert petition filed one day before the extended deadline; disposition pending.
JM-06.stakes: THE gate case. Every crypto bank, fintech trust, and state money experiment needs the Fed's rails; whether access is a right or a favor is now before the Court — or settled for a generation if cert is denied.

JM-07.name: Banco San Juan
JM-07.caption: Banco San Juan Internacional v. FRBNY & Board — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. 25-1144
JM-07.question: May a Reserve Bank terminate an existing master account under contract and risk process?
JM-07.state: Affirmed 2026-05-13: no statutory right to continued service; FRBNY's termination authority stands.
JM-07.stakes: The gate swings both ways — an account once granted can be taken. Second and Tenth Circuits now converge on Reserve Bank discretion.

JM-08.name: Fourth Corner
JM-08.caption: Fourth Corner Credit Union v. FRB Kansas City — D. Colo.; 10th Cir. 16-1016 (2017)
JM-08.question: Must a Reserve Bank serve a state-chartered cannabis credit union?
JM-08.state: Fractured 1-1-1 judgment; amended lawful-purpose complaint allowed; no entitlement established. Later Custodia law rejects the entitlement reading.
JM-08.stakes: The first crack at the gate question — three judges, three theories, no rule — showing why Custodia's published holding matters.

JM-09.name: TNB USA
JM-09.caption: TNB USA v. FRBNY — S.D.N.Y. 1:18-cv-07978 (2020)
JM-09.question: Did FRBNY unlawfully stall a "narrow bank" built to pass interest-on-reserves to depositors?
JM-09.state: Dismissed as unripe (2020) — no final denial, no merits ruling.
JM-09.stakes: The narrow-bank idea — 100%-reserve money without lending — died in the waiting room, not in court. The gate can win by never answering.

JM-10.name: Lacewell
JM-10.caption: Lacewell (NYDFS) v. OCC — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. 19-4271 (2021)
JM-10.question: May the OCC charter a national bank that takes no deposits (the fintech charter)?
JM-10.state: Merits vacated for ripeness — OCC never issued the charter, so its authority remains legally unresolved.
JM-10.stakes: The unanswered question under every new OCC trust and stablecoin charter: nobody yet knows if the nondepository national charter survives a merits fight.

JM-11.name: Cantero
JM-11.caption: Cantero v. Bank of America — SCOTUS 22-529 (2024); 2d Cir. on remand; new petition No. 25-1313
JM-11.question: When does a federal bank charter preempt state financial law?
JM-11.state: 2024: nuanced Barnett-Bank "significant interference" test, no categorical preemption. On remand the bank won again (2026-05-05); a second cert petition is pending.
JM-11.stakes: The method that will decide the GENIUS-era fights — whether a federal stablecoin charter displaces state money-transmission, reserve, and consumer rules.

JM-12.name: Dealer Rule
JM-12.caption: Nat'l Ass'n of Private Fund Managers v. SEC — N.D. Tex. 4:24-cv-00250 (2024)
JM-12.question: Could the SEC define proprietary Treasury-market liquidity providers as "dealers"?
JM-12.state: Rule vacated nationwide (2024-11-21); no appellate reversal located. The separate 2023 central-clearing mandate was NOT vacated.
JM-12.stakes: Drew the perimeter of who must register in the Treasury market just as the clearing mandate rewires it — the plumbing rule survives, the perimeter rule died.

JM-13.name: Van Loon
JM-13.caption: Van Loon v. Treasury/OFAC — W.D. Tex.; 5th Cir. 23-50669 (2024)
JM-13.question: Are immutable smart contracts "property" of a sanctioned person under IEEPA?
JM-13.state: Fifth Circuit: no — immutable code can't be owned or controlled. Treasury delisted Tornado Cash 2025-03-21; the case ended after remand.
JM-13.stakes: The first judicial boundary on sanctioning code itself: OFAC keeps power over people and mutable property, but the protocol layer slipped the blocklist.

JM-14.name: Coin Center
JM-14.caption: Coin Center v. Treasury — N.D. Fla.; 11th Cir. 23-13698
JM-14.question: Parallel Tornado Cash challenge — property theory plus First Amendment claims.
JM-14.state: Argued 2024-11-19; Treasury's delisting changed the operative state mid-appeal.
JM-14.stakes: The twin that never got its own holding — mootness by agency retreat, a pattern this map sees repeatedly.

JM-15.name: IEEPA tariffs
JM-15.caption: Learning Resources v. Trump / Trump v. V.O.S. Selections — SCOTUS 24-1287 & 25-250 (2026)
JM-15.question: Does IEEPA's emergency import power include tariffs?
JM-15.state: Decided 2026-02-20: no — tariff power is a tax power belonging to Congress. Blocking and sanctions authorities expressly distinguished and preserved.
JM-15.stakes: Clipped the broadest emergency-money tool while leaving the sanctions sword intact — the Court drawing lines INSIDE emergency power, not around it.

JM-16.name: Bank Markazi
JM-16.caption: Bank Markazi v. Peterson — SCOTUS 14-770 (2016)
JM-16.question: May Congress write an attachment statute for one identified pile of blocked central-bank assets in pending litigation?
JM-16.state: Upheld 6–2: §8772 changed the governing law without dictating findings; ~$1.75B went to terrorism-judgment creditors.
JM-16.stakes: The precedent that makes "untouchable" sovereign reserves touchable by one statute — the exact template a Russian-assets vesting fight would test.

JM-17.name: Collins
JM-17.caption: Collins v. Yellen — SCOTUS 19-422 (2021)
JM-17.question: Could shareholders unwind the FHFA net-worth sweep, and was the Director's removal protection valid?
JM-17.state: Sweep attack barred by HERA's anti-injunction clause; single-director removal protection unconstitutional but no automatic unwinding without proven harm.
JM-17.stakes: Government took the GSEs' entire profit stream and the courts couldn't touch the act — only the org chart. The purse's hardest lesson.

JM-18.name: Perry Capital
JM-18.caption: Perry Capital v. Lew — D.D.C.; D.C. Cir. (2017)
JM-18.question: Could courts enjoin the Third Amendment net-worth sweep as beyond conservator power?
JM-18.state: No — §4617(f) bars equitable relief while FHFA acts as conservator; contract claims took a separate, narrower path.
JM-18.stakes: The review-bar template: while the conservator works, the courthouse door is shut. Foundational for every future resolution fight.

JM-19.name: New York v. Trump
JM-19.caption: New York (19 states) v. Trump — S.D.N.Y. 1:25-cv-01144; 2d Cir. 25-1860
JM-19.question: Was DOGE-team access to Treasury's central payment systems (and their PII) lawful?
JM-19.state: Modified preliminary injunction: access only for trained, vetted personnel under documented conditions. Appeal pending.
JM-19.stakes: Who may read — and hold — the pipes every federal payment runs through. The operative restraint on payment-system access nationwide.

JM-20.name: Alliance v. Bessent
JM-20.caption: Alliance for Retired Americans v. Bessent — D.D.C. 1:25-cv-00313 (2026)
JM-20.question: Was the same Treasury data access reviewable under the APA?
JM-20.state: Summary judgment for Treasury (2026-03-05): intra-agency access by Treasury employees was not final agency action; ultra-vires review unavailable.
JM-20.stakes: The twin that lost — showing the finality doctrine can swallow a payment-privacy claim whole. The S.D.N.Y. injunction (JM-19) is what actually binds.

JM-21.name: NSBA
JM-21.caption: NSBA v. Yellen — N.D. Ala. (2024); 11th Cir.
JM-21.question: Is the Corporate Transparency Act within Congress's enumerated powers?
JM-21.state: Held unconstitutional as to the named plaintiffs only; appeal's importance faded when Treasury exempted domestic entities (2025).
JM-21.stakes: The constitutional question was never settled nationally — the reporting regime narrowed by agency choice, not judgment, and could widen the same way.

JM-22.name: Texas Top Cop Shop
JM-22.caption: Texas Top Cop Shop v. Garland — E.D. Tex.; 5th Cir.; SCOTUS 24A653
JM-22.question: Could one district court stop CTA beneficial-ownership reporting nationwide?
JM-22.state: Universal injunction stayed by SCOTUS 2025-01-23; FinCEN's 2025-03-26 rule then exempted all domestic entities — the operating state comes from the agency, not a final holding.
JM-22.stakes: The whole domestic ownership-registry question now rests on a revocable rule. The database perimeter is policy, not law.

JM-23.name: Forcht Bank
JM-23.caption: Forcht Bank v. CFPB — E.D. Ky. 5:24-cv-00304; 6th Cir. 25-6164
JM-23.question: Did the 2024 open-banking (§1033) data rule exceed the statute and unlawfully lean on private standard-setters?
JM-23.state: Enforcement enjoined, compliance dates stayed; CFPB is rewriting the rule; appeal open.
JM-23.stakes: Whether Americans' bank-account data becomes portable by mandate — and who writes the technical standards — is suspended mid-air.

JM-24.name: Chatrie
JM-24.caption: Chatrie v. United States — SCOTUS 25-112 (2026); 4th Cir. en banc below
JM-24.question: Is acquiring geofence location data a Fourth Amendment search?
JM-24.state: Yes (2026-06-29). Bank-records doctrine (Miller) expressly not decided.
JM-24.stakes: The first crack in the third-party dam. If the logic reaches financial telemetry, the entire payment-surveillance ledger needs a warrant.

JM-25.name: Culley
JM-25.caption: Culley v. Marshall — SCOTUS 22-585 (2024)
JM-25.question: Does due process require a separate preliminary hearing while seized property awaits forfeiture trial?
JM-25.state: No — a timely merits hearing suffices (6–3).
JM-25.stakes: The state may hold what it seizes for the duration. Applied to digital assets, custody-pending-forfeiture is the whole game (see JM-36).

JM-26.name: Freeman
JM-26.caption: Freeman v. FDIC — D.C. Cir., 56 F.3d 1394 (1995)
JM-26.question: May courts restrain the FDIC's receivership powers?
JM-26.state: Foundational no — §1821(j) bars it unless FDIC acts clearly outside statute; claims go through FIRREA's process.
JM-26.stakes: Resolution happens before litigation finishes, always. The FDIC analogue of the HERA bar — and untested against the 2023-era estates.

JM-27.name: Starr — US
JM-27.caption: Starr International v. United States — Ct. Fed. Cl.; Fed. Cir. (2017); cert denied 2018
JM-27.question: Was taking 79.9% of AIG's equity as rescue consideration authorized by §13(3)?
JM-27.state: Trial court said no but awarded nothing; Federal Circuit vacated the merits ruling (claims belonged to AIG). No binding illegality holding survives.
JM-27.stakes: The government kept everything the rescue took and no precedent says it couldn't — the vacated opinion is a ghost that haunts the next crisis.

JM-28.name: Starr — FRBNY
JM-28.caption: Starr International v. FRBNY — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. (2014)
JM-28.question: Did FRBNY owe Delaware fiduciary duties to AIG shareholders during the rescue?
JM-28.state: No — federal common law displaced conflicting state fiduciary rules for a Reserve Bank's stabilization acts.
JM-28.stakes: A Reserve Bank rescuing the system answers to federal function, not shareholder law — the public/private seam ruled in favor of the public hand.

JM-29.name: Bloomberg
JM-29.caption: Bloomberg L.P. v. Board of Governors — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. (2010); cert denied 2011
JM-29.question: Were crisis-era borrower and loan records disclosable under FOIA?
JM-29.state: Yes — Exemption 4 rejected; the Board released borrower-level records 2011-03-31.
JM-29.stakes: Who borrowed from the lender of last resort became public knowledge only by lawsuit — Dodd-Frank then built delayed disclosure into §13(3) permanently.

JM-30.name: Fox
JM-30.caption: Fox News Network v. Board of Governors — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. (2010)
JM-30.question: Which Reserve-Bank-held records count as Board records for FOIA?
JM-30.state: Further search/disclosure ordered; Bank loan files are not automatically Board records — the structural distinction survives.
JM-30.stakes: The twelve Banks' private corporate form still shields their papers unless the Board holds them — the transparency line runs through the System's hybrid anatomy.

JM-31.name: Chrysler
JM-31.caption: In re Chrysler / Indiana Pensions v. Chrysler — Bankr. S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir.; SCOTUS (2009)
JM-31.question: Was the Treasury-financed §363 sale a sub-rosa plan that trampled secured-creditor priority, funded by TARP beyond its statute?
JM-31.state: Sale closed after a one-day Ginsburg stay; SCOTUS later vacated the appellate opinion as moot. The transaction stands; the precedent doesn't exist.
JM-31.stakes: The rescue playbook: move fast, close the deal, moot the challenge. Secured creditors learned priority bends when Treasury funds the buyer.

JM-32.name: Murray
JM-32.caption: Murray v. Treasury & Board — E.D. Mich.; 6th Cir. (2012)
JM-32.question: Taxpayer Establishment Clause challenge to AIG rescue funds touching Sharia-compliant products.
JM-32.state: Affirmed for the government on standing; no ruling on bailout authority.
JM-32.stakes: Taxpayers as such can't reach the rescue power — standing doctrine guards the purse's outer wall.

JM-33.name: Global Relief
JM-33.caption: Global Relief Foundation v. O'Neill — N.D. Ill.; 7th Cir. (2002); cert denied 2003
JM-33.question: Could OFAC block a U.S. nonprofit's assets pre-hearing, on classified evidence?
JM-33.state: Yes at the preliminary stage — "interest" reads broadly, no pre-seizure hearing required in emergency, ex parte review allowed.
JM-33.stakes: Domestic blocking without title transfer — the entity dies operationally while formally owning everything. The sword's domestic edge.

JM-34.name: Exxon
JM-34.caption: Exxon Mobil v. Mnuchin — N.D. Tex. 3:17-cv-01930 (2019)
JM-34.question: Did OFAC give fair notice that accepting Sechin's signature violated Russia sanctions?
JM-34.state: No — $2M penalty vacated on due-process fair-notice grounds; the sanctions themselves stood.
JM-34.stakes: The sword must speak clearly before it cuts a domestic company — one of the few due-process wins against OFAC.

JM-35.name: Gratkowski
JM-35.caption: United States v. Gratkowski — 5th Cir. 19-50492 (2020)
JM-35.question: Any Fourth Amendment privacy in public blockchain data or exchange KYC records?
JM-35.state: No — blockchain is public; Coinbase records analogized to bank records under Miller.
JM-35.stakes: The tracing pipeline (analytics → exchange records → person) is constitutionally frictionless — unless Chatrie's logic (JM-24) someday reaches it.

JM-36.name: Battle Born
JM-36.caption: United States v. Approximately 69,370 Bitcoin — N.D. Cal.; 9th Cir.; cert denied 2024
JM-36.question: Who owns the Silk Road wallet the government seized?
JM-36.state: Competing claims stricken for lack of proof; government custody stands. No source proves the wallet entered the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.
JM-36.stakes: The largest single BTC hoard in federal hands cleared its ownership contest — the reserve's supply chain runs through forfeiture standing doctrine.

JM-37.name: Celsius
JM-37.caption: In re Celsius Network — Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 22-10964 (2023)
JM-37.question: Did Earn-account customers or the estate own the deposited crypto?
JM-37.state: Terms of use transferred title — Earn assets are estate property; customers hold unsecured claims. Plan effective 2024-01-31.
JM-37.stakes: "Your keys" ended at the click-wrap. The ruling that made custody terms the whole ballgame for every yield platform.

JM-38.name: BlockFi
JM-38.caption: In re BlockFi / Meghji v. United States — Bankr. D.N.J. 22-19361; Adv. 23-01144
JM-38.question: Customer wallets vs. estate; then estate vs. criminal forfeiture (the FTX collision).
JM-38.state: Qualifying Wallet assets = customer property (opposite of Celsius, different terms); government limited to defendants' traceable interests; $35M+ restrained during tracing; final allocation unverified.
JM-38.stakes: Fine print decides whose coins survive a collapse — and when DOJ forfeiture meets a bankruptcy estate, the bankruptcy court holds the boundary.

JM-39.name: Dames & Moore
JM-39.caption: Dames & Moore v. Regan — SCOTUS 453 U.S. 654 (1981)
JM-39.question: Could the President nullify attachments, transfer blocked Iranian assets, and suspend private claims to implement the Algiers Accords?
JM-39.state: Upheld in the narrow setting of congressional acquiescence and long claims-settlement practice.
JM-39.stakes: The root of modern emergency money power — the President can move blocked sovereign assets and reroute private claims when Congress doesn't object.

JM-40.name: NML/BCRA
JM-40.caption: NML Capital v. Banco Central de la República Argentina — S.D.N.Y.; 2d Cir. 652 F.3d 172 (2011)
JM-40.question: Could creditors attach ~$105M of Argentina's central-bank reserves at FRBNY?
JM-40.state: No — FSIA §1611(b)(1) protects central-bank property "held for its own account" regardless of alter-ego analysis.
JM-40.stakes: The FRBNY account as sovereign sanctuary — the rule that makes New York safe for other nations' reserves, and the wall any Russian-assets move must breach.

JM-41.name: Argentina v. NML
JM-41.caption: Republic of Argentina v. NML Capital — SCOTUS 573 U.S. 134 (2014)
JM-41.question: Does the FSIA limit discovery into a sovereign's worldwide assets?
JM-41.state: No — worldwide post-judgment discovery allowed; attachability decided separately.
JM-41.stakes: Creditors may map a sovereign's entire fortune even where they can't yet seize it — surveillance of the hoard precedes the raid.

JM-42.name: Rubin
JM-42.caption: Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran — SCOTUS 16-534 (2018)
JM-42.question: Is FSIA §1610(g) a freestanding exception to execution immunity?
JM-42.state: No, unanimously — creditors need an independent immunity exception; museum-held Persian antiquities stayed immune.
JM-42.stakes: Terrorism judgments don't self-execute against sovereign property — each seizure needs its own statutory door.

JM-43.name: Peterson II
JM-43.caption: Peterson v. Iran, Clearstream, et al. — S.D.N.Y. 1:13-cv-09195; 2d Cir.; cert denied 2025
JM-43.question: Can creditors reach $1.68B in bond proceeds credited in Luxembourg after passing through New York?
JM-43.state: 2026-03-31: turnover summary judgment again granted; implementation report ordered; no verified transfer or new appeal yet.
JM-43.stakes: If this money moves, a foreign central bank's offshore assets will have been taken through New York's rails by court order — the Hoard's live wire.

JM-44.name: Crystallex
JM-44.caption: Crystallex v. Venezuela — D. Del.; 3d Cir. (2019)
JM-44.question: Was PDVSA Venezuela's alter ego, exposing PDV Holding (CITGO) shares to attachment?
JM-44.state: Yes — attachment sustained; the judicial sale process is valid but closing requires a specific OFAC license (FAQ 1246, 2026-03-18).
JM-44.stakes: A U.S. court can queue up a sovereign's crown-jewel company for sale — but Treasury holds the final key. Two gates, two masters.

JM-45.name: OI European
JM-45.caption: OI European Group v. Venezuela — 3d Cir. 23-1647 (2023)
JM-45.question: Did Venezuela's changed governance end PDVSA's alter-ego status?
JM-45.state: No — status persists; more creditors joined the sale queue; no CITGO closing yet.
JM-45.stakes: The creditor queue grows while the OFAC license gate stays shut — a whole hierarchy of claims waiting on one executive signature.

JM-46.name: SVB Financial Trust
JM-46.caption: SVB Financial Trust v. FDIC-R — N.D. Cal. 5:24-cv-01321 (consol.)
JM-46.question: Who bears the holding company's $1.9B of deposits stranded in the receivership — and under what officer-conduct standard?
JM-46.state: Open — $1.7B stipulated baseline subject to setoff/defenses; jury trial set 2026-07-13, San Jose.
JM-46.stakes: The first jury verdict on how the 2023 systemic-risk rescue splits money between the receiver and the estate.

JM-47.name: HK Capital / Signature
JM-47.caption: HK Capital LLC v. FDIC-R — S.D.N.Y. 1:23-cv-03775 (2024)
JM-47.question: Are funds removed years before failure and absent from failure-date books insured or assumed deposits?
JM-47.state: Dismissed — not insured, not assumed; claimant left to residual remedies.
JM-47.stakes: What the books say on failure day is what the insurance covers — no equity backstop behind the ledger.

JM-48.name: Rise Development / Signature
JM-48.caption: Rise Development Partners v. Signature Bank — S.D.N.Y. 1:23-cv-04242
JM-48.question: Do pre-failure litigation liabilities travel to the bridge bank or stay with the receiver?
JM-48.state: FIRREA channel applied — liabilities retained by FDIC-R; no merits payment ordered.
JM-48.stakes: The receiver's channel swallows the lawsuit: sue the estate, wait in line.

JM-49.name: First Republic advisers
JM-49.caption: First Republic Inv. Mgmt. v. Nickel — N.D. Cal. 4:24-cv-02574 (2025)
JM-49.question: Can the acquirer's side stop FINRA counterclaims tied to the failed bank's pre-purchase conduct?
JM-49.state: Dismissed without prejudice as unripe; liability boundary unresolved.
JM-49.stakes: The P&A moved the assets; nobody has yet decided where the old sins live.

JM-50.name: Rodriguez
JM-50.caption: Rodriguez v. FDIC — 589 U.S. 132 (2020)
JM-50.question: Does federal common law decide who owns a consolidated tax refund — receiver or holding-company estate?
JM-50.state: No — Bob Richards rejected; state law and the tax-allocation agreement govern.
JM-50.stakes: Ownership of money inside a failed banking group is contract and state law, not federal invention.

JM-51.name: WaMu intervention
JM-51.caption: Deutsche Bank v. FDIC (Anchorage) — D.C. Cir. 12-5170 (2013)
JM-51.question: May noteholders intervene on a conjectural estate-depletion theory?
JM-51.state: No — standing denied; repurchase-liability allocation left undecided.
JM-51.stakes: The biggest bank failure's creditors couldn't even get in the room.

JM-52.name: Rundgren / WaMu
JM-52.caption: Rundgren v. Washington Mutual — 760 F.3d 1056 (9th Cir. 2014)
JM-52.question: Can pre-receivership claims skip FIRREA's administrative process?
JM-52.stakes: The exhaustion wall: the receiver's paperwork line is the only door.

JM-53.name: BofA / Colonial
JM-53.caption: Bank of America v. Colonial Bank — 604 F.3d 1239 (11th Cir. 2010)
JM-53.question: Can a court enjoin the receiver even over claimed custodial assets?
JM-53.state: No — §1821(j) bars injunctive restraint; money remedies only.
JM-53.stakes: Even 'that's MY property in your vault' cannot stop the receiver mid-resolution.

JM-54.name: Waterview
JM-54.caption: Waterview Mgmt. v. FDIC — 105 F.3d 696 (D.C. Cir. 1997)
JM-54.question: What survives when the receiver repudiates a contract?
JM-54.state: Direct compensatory damages under §1821(e) survive; performance does not.
JM-54.stakes: Repudiate-and-pay: the receiver breaks promises lawfully and settles in claims currency.

JM-55.name: Whistler / DTCC
JM-55.caption: Whistler Investments v. DTCC — 9th Cir. 06-16088 (2008)
JM-55.question: Do state-law duties inconsistent with SEC-approved clearing rules survive?
JM-55.state: No — conflict preemption; field preemption and blanket immunity rejected.
JM-55.stakes: The clearing rulebook carries federal armor wherever the SEC has blessed it.

JM-56.name: International Power / DTC lock
JM-56.caption: In re International Power Group — SEC Rel. 34-66611 (2012)
JM-56.question: May DTC globally lock an issuer without notice and a record?
JM-56.state: No — fair procedure required; substantive gatekeeping power left intact.
JM-56.stakes: The depository's chokepoint is real; the SEC only made it keep minutes.

JM-57.name: Susquehanna / OCC capital
JM-57.caption: Susquehanna Int'l Group v. SEC — D.C. Cir. 16-1061 (2017)
JM-57.question: Was the SEC's approval of the options clearinghouse's capital plan adequately reasoned?
JM-57.state: No — arbitrary; remanded WITHOUT vacatur; the plan kept running.
JM-57.stakes: The regulator failed and the utility kept the money — how CCP capital fights actually end.

JM-58.name: U.S. Futures Exchange
JM-58.caption: USFE v. CBOT/CME — 7th Cir. 18-3558 (2020)
JM-58.question: Does a CFTC-reviewed open-interest transfer get antitrust immunity?
JM-58.state: Yes on this record — implied immunity via active regulatory review.
JM-58.stakes: Competition law bends where the regulator has actively looked — the clearing moat is legal.

JM-59.name: MF Global
JM-59.caption: In re MF Global Inc. — Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 11-02790 (2011–)
JM-59.question: How far does commodity-customer property protection reach when an FCM fails?
JM-59.state: Transfers/settlements restored customer value; priority did not reach the holding-company estate.
JM-59.stakes: Segregation is the promise; the pool and the transfers are what customers actually got.

JM-60.name: Merit Management
JM-60.caption: Merit Management v. FTI Consulting — 583 U.S. 366 (2018)
JM-60.question: Does passing a transfer through banks/clearing intermediaries shield it under §546(e)?
JM-60.state: No — the conduit does not protect the overarching transfer; unanimous.
JM-60.stakes: The plumbing is not a laundry: routing money through the rails buys no safe harbor.

JM-61.name: Alpine / NSCC
JM-61.caption: Alpine Securities v. NSCC — 10th Cir. 25-4050 (argued 2026-01-21)
JM-61.question: Is NSCC's member discipline state action subject to constitutional limits?
JM-61.state: District said no likely state action; dismissed; appeal argued and UNDECIDED.
JM-61.stakes: The live one: whether the private clearinghouse wielding compulsory power is the state — asked while the mandate makes membership compulsory.

JM-62.name: Donmar / Fedwire
JM-62.caption: Donmar Enterprises v. Southern Nat'l Bank — 64 F.3d 944 (4th Cir. 1995)
JM-62.question: Does Regulation J/Article 4A displace state claims over a completed Fedwire transfer?
JM-62.stakes: The federal rail carries its own law; state negligence claims die at the on-ramp.

JM-63.name: Grain Traders
JM-63.caption: Grain Traders v. Citibank — 160 F.3d 97 (2d Cir. 1998)
JM-63.question: Who may recover when a multibank transfer fails midstream?
JM-63.state: Link-by-link privity — refund from your own receiving bank only; final.
JM-63.stakes: No end-runs down the chain: each link answers only to its neighbor.

JM-64.name: Banque Worms
JM-64.caption: Banque Worms v. BankAmerica — 77 N.Y.2d 362 (1991)
JM-64.question: May a creditor keep a mistaken wire paying a debt actually due?
JM-64.state: Yes — discharge for value, absent notice of the mistake.
JM-64.stakes: The 12:36 AM wire that wrote the rule every mistaken-payment fight cites.

JM-65.name: Citibank / Revlon
JM-65.caption: In re Citibank Aug. 11, 2020 Wire Transfers — 2d Cir. 21-487 (2022)
JM-65.question: Could the Revlon lenders keep Citibank's mistaken $894M principal release?
JM-65.state: No — inquiry notice defeated discharge for value; funds returned after remand.
JM-65.stakes: The wire is final but the keeping is not — the biggest fat-finger in rail history came back.

JM-66.name: Sheerbonnet / BCCI
JM-66.caption: Sheerbonnet v. American Express Bank — S.D.N.Y. 92 Civ. 7426
JM-66.question: Does Article 4A displace claims over a wire knowingly credited to a frozen account?
JM-66.state: Partly survived displacement; ultimate disposition needs docket verification.
JM-66.stakes: The seam between the freeze and the rail: money that arrived after the padlock.

JM-67.name: Consarc / Iraq
JM-67.caption: Consarc Corp. v. Iraqi Ministry — 27 F.3d 695 (D.C. Cir. 1994)
JM-67.question: Can a court compel OFAC to license execution against blocked funds?
JM-67.state: No — reversal; the license gate is Treasury's alone.
JM-67.stakes: Blocking preserves the money without deciding whose it is — and only Treasury opens the door.

JM-68.name: Calderon-Cardona
JM-68.caption: Calderon-Cardona v. BNY Mellon — 770 F.3d 993 (2d Cir. 2014)
JM-68.question: Who owns a blocked midstream EFT for TRIA/FSIA execution?
JM-68.state: Nobody en route — chain-specific sender ownership controls; remanded.
JM-68.stakes: The rule that made blocked wires nearly judgment-proof.

JM-69.name: Levin
JM-69.caption: Estate of Levin v. Wells Fargo — D.C. Cir. 21-7036 (2022)
JM-69.question: Is Article 4A the federal rule for blocked-EFT execution under TRIA?
JM-69.state: No — TRIA tracing allowed where no innocent intermediary claims the funds.
JM-69.stakes: Washington's answer against New York's — the blocked-EFT law is now a live circuit tension.

JM-70.name: Philpott
JM-70.caption: Philpott v. Essex County Welfare Bd. — 409 U.S. 413 (1973)
JM-70.question: May a state reach Social Security funds after deposit?
JM-70.state: No — §407 protects them in the account.
JM-70.stakes: The oldest stone in the wall around federal benefit money.

JM-71.name: Bennett
JM-71.caption: Bennett v. Arkansas — 485 U.S. 395 (1988)
JM-71.question: May a state attach a prisoner's Social Security benefits?
JM-71.stakes: The benefits wall holds against the states a second time.

JM-72.name: Lockhart
JM-72.caption: Lockhart v. United States — 546 U.S. 142 (2005)
JM-72.question: May Treasury offset Social Security for old federal debts notwithstanding §407?
JM-72.stakes: The wall stops garnishment at the bank but not withholding at the spigot — the pre-disbursement control point, named twenty years before the payment-integrity fights.
